title: Rama walks into the Sarayu
hookLine: the Ramayana's last scene, and the devotee who stays wherever it's told
carry: where rama's story is told, hanuman is there
tomorrow: why do Hindus wait up till midnight for a baby?

lines: A WEDDING, A WAR, A HOMECOMING.
cards: Months ago, at the start of this serial, by a river, a hunter's arrow brought down a bird, and Valmiki's grief turned into the first verse.
Since then: a bow broken at a wedding, a forest, a golden deer, a leap across the sea, a war, a homecoming, and a later book that won't let the homecoming be the end.
Today, how the poem itself finally stops, and who it leaves behind.

teach.b: After Sita is gone, Valmiki's poem goes on a little longer. Rama rules alone, for many years.
Back when he was crowned, he had said goodbye to his allies one by one, and when it was Hanuman's turn, Hanuman asked for only one thing.

teach.h: AS LONG AS YOUR STORY IS TOLD.
teach.b: Let my love for you never waver, he said, and let me live on earth as long as your story is told. Rama granted it. Now Rama's own time on earth is complete.
He walks out of Ayodhya toward the river Sarayu, and the people of the city follow him, unwilling to stay behind. He walks into the water, and returns to his own form as Vishnu.
That's the last image: a king walking into a river. But one devotee doesn't follow. Rama reminds Hanuman of his wish: stay, as long as my story is told.
So the Ramayana ends with a gift. Wherever it's recited, devotees believe Hanuman is listening.

That's why, at many Ramayana readings, people keep a seat empty for him, sometimes with a cloth and a flower on it. And it's the deeper reason the story is still told, even with an ending people argue over.
For devotees, telling it isn't only remembering. It's a place where God's greatest devotee is present, and through him, Rama. The avatar went home.

teach.h: THE STORY STAYED, AND SO DID HANUMAN.
teach.b: The story stayed, and Hanuman stayed with it.

teach.h: WHERE RAMA'S STORY IS TOLD, HANUMAN IS THERE.
teach.b: Many teachers read Hanuman as bhakti, loving devotion, at its plainest: a love that asks only to stay near God's name.
So when a grandmother reads the Ramayana aloud in a living room, devotees would say that room isn't ordinary anymore.

how: Many Hindu households recite the Ramayana or its Sundara Kanda on special occasions, and at many readings a seat is kept for Hanuman, who is said to listen wherever Rama's story is told; the later book is read, told or argued over in many different ways.

s: Hanuman asks to stay on earth as long as Rama's story is told
Rama grants it, and many readings still keep a seat for him.
Valmiki's poem ends at the moment the earth takes Sita
it goes on: Rama rules alone, and at the end walks into the Sarayu.
for devotees, reciting the Ramayana is only remembering the past
many believe Hanuman is listening wherever it's told, so a reading is a place of devotion, not just memory.

games.q: you're at a Ramayana reading and see an empty cushion up front with a flower on it. a friend goes to sit there. what fits today?
o: gently stop them: many keep that seat for Hanuman, who listens wherever the story is told.
let them; empty seats are for latecomers.
move the flower; it's just decoration.
games.why: Hanuman asked to live as long as Rama's story is told. so where it's read, devotees save him a place.

practice: Sit comfortably and let one image from the whole Ramayana come up on its own: a bow, a deer, a ring, a bridge, a furrow. If you pray, say Rama's name, or Sita Ram, slowly a few times, and picture Hanuman listening, as he promised.
If you don't, keep the image company, and think of whoever first told you this story.

wordCard.voice: Sarayu. The river of Ayodhya, where Rama ends his earthly life and returns as Vishnu, leaving Hanuman behind with the story.

orig.note: Sanskrit sarayū: the river of Ayodhya, where Rama ends his earthly life.
